name: Kamas-Koibal
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Kuennap, Ago. 1999. Kamass (Languages of the World/Materials 185).

new_statements.quote: § 12. Über die Akzentuierung der kamassischen Wörter schreibt Donner: »Der exspiratorische akzent ist gewöhnlich unbezeichnet gelassen, da er meistens auf der ersten silbe ruht. Doch kann er auch, am nächsten unter dem einfluss des tatarischen, wechseln und auf der letzten silbe des wortes liegen. Wenn der vokal der zweiten silbe lang ist, oder an dieser stelle ein diphthong steht, hat die zweite silbe den hauptakzent. Bisweilen, nicht aber regelmässig, ruht ein nebenakzent auf der dritten silbe» (Anl. S. VII). [...] Sowohl im Wb. als in den Sprachproben sind eine Menge Ausnahmen und Schwankungen von diesen Regeln festzustellen.
new_statements.translation: § 12. On the accentuation of Kamassian words Donner writes: 'The expiratory accent is usually left unmarked, since it mostly rests on the first syllable. But it can also, most probably under the influence of Tatar, shift and lie on the last syllable of the word. If the vowel of the second syllable is long, or a diphthong stands in that position, the second syllable has the main accent. Sometimes, but not regularly, a secondary accent rests on the third syllable' (Anl. p. VII). [...] Both in the dictionary and in the text specimens a great many exceptions to and fluctuations from these rules are to be found.
new_statements.citation: Joki, Aulis J. (ed.). 1944. Kai Donners Kamassisches Wörterbuch nebst Sprachproben und Hauptzügen der Grammatik. Lexica Societatis Fenno-Ugricae VIII. Helsinki: Suomalais-ugrilainen Seura.
new_statements.locator: Hauptzüge der Grammatik, Lautlehre, 'III. Der Akzent', § 12, pp. 126-127 (PDF p. 182-183 of the Fenno-Ugrica scan; p. 126 verified on the page image)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default main (expiratory) accent on the first syllable; if the second syllable has a long vowel or diphthong (Klumpp 2016: if the first syllable is light and a following syllable heavy) the main accent moves to that heavy syllable. A competing Turkic-type final accent (Donner: under Tatar influence; Klumpp: a pitch accent coexisting with the expiratory pattern) appears in loans and some native words; in disyllables the accent is described as free between 1st and 2nd syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Donner (as quoted by Joki, p. 126): sometimes, not regularly, a secondary accent on the third syllable; in polysyllabic words main accent on the 1st and secondary accent on the 3rd syllable. Joki notes Donner's colon notation (e.g. örəme:) probably marks a secondary accent. Klumpp 2016 p. 43 reads such notations as coexistence of first-syllable main stress with Turkic ultima accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Joki pp. 126-127: main accent may sit on the 2nd syllable even without a long vowel/diphthong (e.g. ei sura·rga 'he does not ask', ťådå·ľam 'to fill'); loanword accent does not always follow the source language (kartüz < Russ. kartuz, stenā < Russ. stená); accent can even rest on an overshort reduced vowel; Tatarized Kamassians tend to put the accent always on the last syllable; in disyllables pronounced in isolation the accent very often falls on the 2nd syllable, especially in Tatar loans.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level expiratory accent in Donner's 1912-1914 field data (dictionary entries and text specimens); Donner explicitly notes that words 'pronounced in isolation' (citation form) often show 2nd-syllable accent in disyllables. Klumpp 2016 pp. 42-43 restates the same three patterns for Kamas as a whole and treats the ultima pattern as pitch accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Statement concerns Kamas proper (Kamassian) as recorded by Kai Donner in 1912-1914 at Abalakovo (Sayan region), the language of the Glottolog language-level entry kama1351 'Kamas-Koibal'; Koibal itself is known only from 18th-century wordlists and has no accent data. Klumpp 2016 treats the same Kamas data. The post-shift Kamas of the last speaker Klavdiya Plotnikova (recorded 1960s-1980s; Klooster 2015) is a later, heavily russianized stage and is not described for stress.

sources.note: 'III. Der Akzent' § 12, pp. 126-127 (PDF p. 182, page image checked): quoting Donner, expiratory accent usually on the first syllable; a long vowel or diphthong in the second syllable takes the main accent; under Tatar (Turkic) influence accent may fall on the last syllable; in disyllables the accent is 'free' between 1st and 2nd (often 2nd in isolation, esp. Tatar loans); in polysyllables main on 1st, secondary on 3rd; many exceptions and fluctuations noted in the dictionary and texts.

sources.note: Unit 3 Phonology §3 'Syllable structure and accent', pp. 42-43: 'The (probably inherited) pattern of assigning prominency to the first syllable of a word by expiratory accent, e.g. ka·m.bi went, is challenged by two divergent patterns: (i) if the first syllable is light (open, short or reduced vowel), and a following syllable heavy (closed, long vowel) accent moves to the heavy syllable, e.g. su.ra·r.ga asking, a.mo·r.zit.tǝ to eat; (ii) the Turkic pattern of assigning accent to the last syllable has been noticed by Castrén and Donner (KW: 126-127), not only in Turkish loans, but also in genu…
